<reason>Both sides argued at a high level, but CON built and held the cleaner decisive frame: the motion is redundant where slack already exists and harmful where hours literally are output. CON's sharpest move was seizing PRO's own concession that employers "simply pay overtime or hire" [A2.3] and showing it splits PRO's case — either the fifth shift vanishes (service rationed) or it survives at a premium, in which case the delivered content of the motion for the carer is a higher wage bill plus hope, not a four-day week. PRO answered honestly (phased budgets, deliberately chosen public spending, defaults shift norms over a generation), and its best counter — that the status quo's cost is paid invisibly in worker endurance — was genuinely strong weighing. But it conceded the cost rather than dissolving it, and never squarely answered CON's supply point that a vacancy is not an unfilled desire to hire, so mandating that each nurse cover four-fifths of her current load does not conjure a fifth nurse. CON also correctly noted that PRO's historical analogies (eight-hour day, weekend) drop the operative clause of this motion: a statutory guarantee that base pay not adjust. PRO's best route was the coordination/default argument and the "the sequence has a name: never" line, which landed rhetorically; CON blunted it by offering sectoral bargaining and productivity-first sequencing, and by pointing out that a mandate cannot transfer slack to workplaces that lack it. Pressure questions were used well by both, but CON's funding question extracted a concession that shaped the endgame, while PRO's question to CON received a workable (if late-arriving) alternative-mechanism answer. PRO also carried more clipping/execution cost, including a closing cut mid-sentence.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's exploitation of PRO's overtime concession [B2.1-B2.2, B3.2]: if the carer still works five shifts, the motion delivers only a costlier fifth day, so the mandate is either priced-not-delivered or rationing service — PRO could not claim both that output holds and that nothing gets more expensive.</best_rebuttal>
